evidence.quote: An instance consists of a finite directed multigraph $G=(V,E)$ with $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $n\ge1$, and at least one outgoing edge at every vertex. The vertex set is partitioned as $$V=V_{\max}\sqcup V_{\min}\sqcup V_{\mathrm{ch}}.$$ Each edge $e$ has an integer reward $w(e)$. At a vertex of $V_{\max}$, Max chooses the next edge; at a vertex of $V_{\min}$, Min chooses it; at a vertex $i\in V_{\mathrm{ch}}$, the next edge is drawn from a prescribed rational probability distribution $p_i$ on the outgoing edges. Rewards and the numerators and positive denominators of the probabilities are encoded in binary. The graph and all edge data are listed explicitly. Loops, parallel edges, zero probabilities, and unreduced fractions are permitted.

Every subsolution $y$ and supersolution $z$ in the same box satisfy $y\le z$. Starting at $t^0=u$, the iteration $$t^{m+1}=T(t^m),\qquad
 T(t)=\min\{u,\max\{A,\lfloor F(t)\rfloor\}\},
 \label{eq:label-floor}$$ stops at a vector $t^*$ after at most $nD+1$ evaluations of $T$. For every such pair $y,z$ one has $y\le t^*\le z$.

Every child input is valid and its box lies inside its parent’s box. If the child calls terminate, each pivot pass makes at most $1024n+1$ calls. The width base case makes at most $522240n+1$ evaluations of $\lfloor F\rfloor$.

Let $P,Q$ be opposite players in an arena $H$.*

1.  *If $D$ is a $P$-dominion in $H$ and $R$ is a restriction closed at $P$’s vertices, then $D\cap R$ is a $P$-dominion in $R$.*

2.  *If $R$ is closed at $P$’s vertices, every $Q$-dominion in $R$ is a $Q$-dominion in $H$.*

3.  *If $D$ is a $P$-dominion in $H$ and $D\cap X=\varnothing$, then removing $\operatorname{Attr}_Q^H(X)$ leaves $D$ intact and still a $P$-dominion in the residual arena.

Let $H$ be a nonempty arena, and let $d\geq0$ be an integer such that $p(v)\geq d$ for every $v\in H$. Define $$\begin{gathered} P=\begin{cases}\ensuremath{\mathrm{Max}},&d\text{ even},\\\ensuremath{\mathrm{Min}},&d\text{ odd},\end{cases} \qquad S=\{v\in H:p(v)=d\},\\ A=\operatorname{Attr}_P^H(S),\qquad R=H\setminus A. \end{gathered}$$ The set $S$ is allowed to be empty.* 1. *If $d$ is odd and $\mathrm{Min}$ wins everywhere in the game on $R$, then $\mathrm{Min}$ wins everywhere in $H$.* 2. *If $d$ is even, $\mathrm{Max}$ wins for mean payoff alone everywhere in $H$, and from every vertex of $R$ $\mathrm{Max}$ has a conjunction-winning strategy in $R$ satisfying [eq:uniform-prefix], then from every vertex of $H$ $\mathrm{Max}$ has a conjunction-winning strategy satisfying [eq:uniform-prefix].

In every finite arena, each vertex is winning for exactly one of $\mathrm{Max}$ and $\mathrm{Min}$. From each vertex winning for $\mathrm{Max}$, there is a conjunction-winning strategy satisfying [eq:uniform-prefix].

Let $H$ be a nonempty arena and $d\geq0$ an integer such that $p(v)\geq d$ for all $v\in H$. Let $P=\ensuremath{\mathrm{Max}}$ if $d$ is even and $P=\ensuremath{\mathrm{Min}}$ if $d$ is odd, and let $Q$ be the other player. Put $$S=\{v\in H:p(v)=d\},\qquad
 R=H\setminus\operatorname{Attr}_P^H(S).$$ If $d$ is even, assume that $\mathrm{Max}$ wins for mean payoff alone everywhere in $H$. Then every nonempty $Q$-dominion $D$ in $H$ contains a nonempty $Q$-dominion of the game on $R$. The conclusion allows $S=\varnothing$.

For every subarena $H$ of the original game and every $\mathbf b\in\{0,\ldots,n\}^2$, the procedure $\operatorname{Solve}(H,\mathbf b)$ terminates and returns a partition satisfying [eq:label-guarantee] for both players.

For an arena with $n\ge1$ vertices and complete binary input length $L$, the call $\operatorname{Solve}(G,(n,n))$ makes $$2^{O((\log_2(n+2))^2)}$$ calls to the ordinary mean-payoff winning-set subroutine. Each such call has an explicit input of length $(L+2)^{O(1)}$. Apart from those subroutine calls, the computation takes $$2^{O((\log_2(n+2))^2)}(L+2)^{O(1)}$$ bit operations. All constants are absolute.
